title: The Software Pilot That Never Ends

Building software for multifamily operations teams. Writing about SaaS, ops, and the road from zero to Series A. Charlotte, NC. Multifamily Plotline Proptech B2b Saas Product Strategy The Software Pilot That Never Ends Cole Lamphere 5 min read · Oct 9, 2026 -- Listen Share Two properties, a kickoff call, and eleven months later nobody can say who decides. Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Diogo Cardoso on Unsplash A regional in Nashville emailed me in August with one line. Are we still piloting you. Her portfolio had two properties running our software since the previous October. Eleven months. Nobody had ended the pilot and nobody had bought anything. She was not being rude. She genuinely did not know, and neither did the person at corporate who had asked for it, because he moved to a different role in March. A pilot in this industry has a shape. Once you have watched enough of them you can call the steps in order before they happen. It starts at a conference, usually in a hallway. Somebody from corporate sees a demo, likes it, and asks for a pilot rather than a price. The request is reasonable on its face, and it is also the first place the thing goes wrong, because a pilot is a project and nobody has been assigned to run it yet. Then the properties get chosen. They are almost never the two properties with the problem. They are the two with the most agreeable managers, the ones who say yes to corporate without a fight. A 1,100 unit operator in Tampa gave us their two best run assets last year, both above 96 percent, both with a full office and a maintenance tech who had been there nine years. Of course the software looked fine. That pilot was never going to tell anyone anything about the eight properties where the office is one person deep and the make ready board has not been touched since Thursday. Then the kickoff call. Nine people on the invite, six of whom never appear again. Someone from IT asks about single sign on. Someone from accounting asks whether this touches the general ledger. Nobody asks what would have to be true in ninety days for this to become a contract. Then training, which lands on a Tuesday at two in the afternoon, the worst hour in a leasing office. Two leasing consultants attend. One of them is covering the phones while she watches. Then the quiet part. The champion is a regional with four properties and her own quarterly goals, and nothing about this pilot moves her number. Turn season starts. A property changes managers. The 60 day evaluation becomes 120 days, and 120 becomes whenever somebody brings it up again. And nobody ever says no. That is the part I misread for years. I kept reading silence as a slow yes, because the account was still open, still logging in a little, still answering email. We counted the hours once during a cleanup in the spring. Three pilots that had run past eight months had taken about 230 hours of our team time, most of it support and training, all of it against $0 of revenue. Two of the three eventually signed. One is still open today, technically, which is to say it is dead and nobody wants to be the person who says so. Here is the claim a procurement director will push back on. A pilot with no decision date and no named decider works as a free trial with a project manager attached, and the project manager is usually a regional who never asked for the job. I have written before about the software nobody on site opens . A pilot is where that story starts, because a pilot is where a product first meets an ordinary Tuesday instead of a demo. But adoption gets blamed for a lot of dead pilots that died of something else. The team using the software cannot buy it, and the people who can buy it are not in the room. I have argued that the regional manager is the real buyer , and during a pilot she is also the only person being asked to add work to a week that is already full, with no budget attached and no deadline to point at. This is the part no product team can fix. You can build better onboarding, faster setup, in app guidance, a cleaner first week. We have built all of it. None of it supplies a decision date, and none of it tells an organization who gets to decide. That is governance, and it sits several floors above the leasing office where the software actually runs. So we changed what we agree to. Pilots run 45 days now, with three things written down before day one: the name of the person who decides, the date they decide, and the two numbers that count as pass or fail. Usually those numbers are days to rent ready and the age of the oldest open work order. If an operator will not name a date or a decider, we send a price instead and let them buy or walk. That position costs money. We lost two deals last year to vendors happy to run open ended pilots, and one of them was a 4,000 unit portfolio I wanted badly. A founder could tell me I am being precious about process while a competitor sits in the building collecting usage data, and that is a fair hit. My read is that the vendor who settles into a nine month pilot is paying for the privilege of being compared to an incumbent nobody intends to replace. The honest caveat is that some pilots are real, and the real ones are easy to spot. The operator picks a property that has the actual problem. Somebody with signing authority shows up to the kickoff. The dates survive turn season. Those pilots close at a rate that makes the rest of them look like what they are. If you run a portfolio, run fewer pilots and run them on your worst property, with a date on the calendar and your own name beside it. If you sell software, stop counting a pilot request as a win.
